documents.title: Rheumatology follow-up letter
documents.author: rheumatology
documents.body:
Outside rheumatology practice. Date of visit: 02/08/2021.

Dear Doctor,

I saw Ms. Diallo, 44, in follow-up for systemic lupus erythematosus.

Over the last several months she has felt persistently fatigued, with aching in many joints and occasional low-grade fevers. She also describes skin changes after sun exposure and mouth sores that keep coming back.

Current medications: hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily, prednisone 10 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg, amlodipine 5 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, cholecalciferol 2000 units, calcium carbonate 600 mg twice daily. Apart from these she uses an over-the-counter pain reliever only occasionally.
Allergies: sulfonamides (severe rash).

On exam she looked tired but comfortable. There was faint erythema across the malar area. Both wrists had mild synovial fullness. I saw a few shallow ulcers on the buccal mucosa. Heart and lung exams were normal.

Labs today show a mild normocytic anemia and a positive ANA. Creatinine and urinalysis are normal, with no sign of renal involvement.

Assessment: SLE with ongoing constitutional, mucocutaneous and joint symptoms. Given more than a decade of continuous glucocorticoid exposure she should be regarded as immunosuppressed; I have added this to her problem list and would ask that she be vaccinated accordingly and that infections be evaluated with a low threshold.

Plan: continue hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily and prednisone 10 mg daily. I will see her again in the summer.

Rheumatology

documents.title: Hypertension Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Back for BP. Rheum saw her in Feb for fatigue and joint aches. Says she takes the amlodipine, lisinopril and HCTZ every day, pharmacy fill history agrees. No headache, chest pain or palpitations. Brought log: mostly 145-155/90s. Still following a very strict low-salt diet she started on her own years ago - no added salt, low-sodium everything.

O: BP 154/96, HR 78. Looks well hydrated. Lungs clear, heart regular. No edema.
Labs 5/4: Na 146, K 3.1, Cl 108, HCO3 32, Cr 0.9. Plasma renin activity 7.4 (high), aldosterone 26 (high).

A/P:
1. Hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with high renin and high aldosterone on ACEi + thiazide in the setting of severe dietary sodium restriction -> secondary hyperaldosteronism. Pattern is not one of primary aldosteronism (renin is high, not suppressed).
 - Start KCl ER 20 mEq daily.
 - Ease off the extreme salt restriction to ordinary moderate intake (normal cooking, still avoid processed/very salty foods). Discussed at length; she was surprised.
 - BMP 2 wks.
2. HTN, not at goal on 3 drugs. Keep same doses for now, reassess after K corrected and diet adjusted.

RTC 3 months, sooner prn.

documents.title: Orthopedic surgery consultation
documents.author: orthopedics
documents.body:
Outside orthopedic surgery. Seen 1/31/2022.

RE: Aisha Diallo, DOB 07/18/1976

Thank you for sending her back. She has known avascular necrosis of the right femoral head, treated with core decompression in 2019, and now has three months of worsening right hip pain: a dull ache that builds with weight-bearing and settles with rest. No injury. She has taken prednisone 20 mg daily for the past six months.

Meds: hydroxychloroquine, prednisone 20 mg, lisinopril, amlodipine, HCTZ, potassium, vitamin D, calcium. Allergy: sulfonamides.

Exam: walks with an antalgic gait. Right hip range of motion is reduced, internal rotation most of all. The joint is not warm, red or swollen. Neurovascularly intact distally.

Imaging: I reviewed the radiographs from 1/12, which show no fracture or dislocation, and the MRI from 1/21, which shows a crescent sign consistent with subchondral fracture and marrow edema in the femoral head.

Assessment: progression of right femoral head AVN to subchondral collapse.

Plan: I explained that at this stage a repeat core decompression is unlikely to help and that total hip arthroplasty is the definitive treatment. She would like to hold off for now. Cane in the left hand, protected weight-bearing, acetaminophen as needed. I'd encourage the lowest prednisone dose her lupus allows and have written to her rheumatologist. Return when she is ready to talk about surgery, or sooner if pain becomes unmanageable.

Orthopedic Surgery

documents.title: Emergency department physician record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital ED. Seen 01/27/2023 13:40.

CC: sharp left upper abdominal pain.

HPI: 46-year-old woman with SLE on hydroxychloroquine and prednisone, with sudden onset of sharp, constant LUQ pain that goes up into the left shoulder. No trauma or fall. Never had anything like this.

Meds: hydroxychloroquine, prednisone, lisinopril 20, amlodipine 5, HCTZ 25, cholecalciferol, calcium carbonate. Allergy: sulfonamides.

Vitals: T 37.8 C, BP 130/85, HR 95, RR 18.
Exam: uncomfortable, holding still. LUQ tender to palpation, positive splenic percussion sign. No peritoneal rigidity at triage. Heart tachy-normal, regular. Lungs clear.

Labs: Hgb 12.1, WBC 9.0, Plt 250, INR 1.0, LDH elevated, smear without schistocytes.
US: wedge-shaped hypoechoic splenic area. CT A/P with contrast: splenic capsular rupture, perisplenic hematoma and hemoperitoneum.

MDM: atraumatic splenic rupture with hemoperitoneum in an immunosuppressed patient. Two large-bore IVs, type and screen. General surgery at bedside; to OR.

Disposition: admitted to surgery.

documents.title: Operative report - splenectomy
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
Date of surgery: 01/27/2023.
Preoperative and postoperative diagnosis: atraumatic splenic rupture with hemoperitoneum.
Procedure: splenectomy.
Anesthesia: general endotracheal.

Findings: moderate hemoperitoneum evacuated. Spleen with capsular disruption and adherent clot. No accessory spleen seen. Remaining abdominal viscera grossly normal.

The splenic hilum was controlled and divided and the spleen removed and sent to pathology. Hemostasis confirmed, left upper quadrant irrigated, fascia and skin closed.
EBL as recorded by anesthesia. No transfusion. No complications. To PACU stable.

documents.title: Discharge summary
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
Admitted 01/27/2023, discharged 01/31/2023.

Diagnosis: atraumatic splenic rupture with hemoperitoneum, status post splenectomy 1/27.

Course: presented through the ED with acute LUQ pain; CT confirmed splenic rupture with hemoperitoneum; splenectomy the same day. Postoperative Hgb 10.4 on POD 1 and stable after. Diet advanced, ambulating, pain controlled on oral medication. Pathology: capsular rupture with hemorrhagic infarction, no neoplasm.

Discharge meds: home medications unchanged (hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily, prednisone 10 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg, amlodipine 5 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, potassium chloride 20 mEq, cholecalciferol, calcium carbonate). Oxycodone-acetaminophen 5/325, 1 tab q6h prn severe pain, #12. Acetaminophen otherwise.
Allergies: sulfonamides.

Follow-up: PCP within 1 week, to give post-splenectomy vaccines (meningococcal ACWY and B, Haemophilus b; pneumococcal status per PCP) at about 2 weeks after surgery. Fever above 38.3 C now warrants urgent evaluation given asplenia. Surgery clinic 2 weeks. No lifting over 10 lb for 4 weeks.

documents.title: Post-discharge call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Called pt day after discharge. Sore at incision, taking Tylenol, used the oxycodone once overnight. Eating, BM yesterday. No fever. Husband home with her this week. Reviewed fever precautions with no spleen. Appt with PCP Monday 2/6 for wound check and vaccines. Records received from hospital and routed.

documents.title: Post-hospital Visit

Outside psychiatry clinic. Seen 03/28/2023.

Dear Doctor,

Thank you for the urgent referral. Ms. Diallo is a 46-year-old woman with SLE, avascular necrosis of the right femoral head, and a splenectomy two months ago for an atraumatic rupture. She came with her husband.

He describes two weeks of behavior that is out of character: she is irritable, sleeps very little, talks about big plans, and has been spending a lot of money online. Prednisone was raised to high dose about a month ago for a severe lupus flare. She has never had anything like this before. No prior psychiatric history, no substance use.

Vitals in clinic were normal. On exam she was restless and agitated, easily pulled off topic, with rapid pressured speech. Oriented. No psychotic content elicited. Denied suicidal or homicidal thoughts.

Labs drawn today: Hgb 13.2, WBC 7.8, Plt 250, creatinine 0.9, urinalysis normal, TSH 2.5.

Assessment: glucocorticoid-induced neuropsychiatric symptoms with manic features. No evidence of a primary mood disorder, infection or metabolic cause.

Plan:
- Quetiapine 25 mg at bedtime.
- I spoke with her rheumatologist, who agrees to a faster prednisone taper: 40 mg from tomorrow, then 30, 20 and 15 mg weekly, reaching 10 mg daily in about four weeks.
- Husband to manage finances for now. Return precautions given.
- I will see her again in six weeks.

Psychiatry

documents.title: Emergency department record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Hospital emergency department, arrival 03/29/2024 19:20 by ambulance after a seizure at home.

HPI: 47F with SLE on chronic immunosuppression (hydroxychloroquine, prednisone 10 mg), status post splenectomy. Husband reports a week of worsening confusion and trouble with her vision, plus headaches; this evening a seizure at home, her first ever.

Meds: hydroxychloroquine 200 bid, prednisone 10, lisinopril 20, amlodipine 5, HCTZ 25, KCl 20 mEq, cholecalciferol, calcium carbonate. Allergy: sulfonamides.

Exam: afebrile, vitals stable. Post-ictal at first, then slowly clearing but still disoriented to date. Left-sided weakness and poor coordination on the left. Fundi normal. Neck supple, no meningismus.

Workup: HIV screen negative. MRI brain with contrast: one well-circumscribed ring-enhancing lesion in the right parietal lobe, little edema. LP unremarkable.

MDM: new seizure and focal deficit from a solitary enhancing lesion in an immunosuppressed, asplenic host. Differential lymphoma vs infection vs other neoplasm. Levetiracetam loaded, then 500 mg twice daily. Neurosurgery and oncology consulted.

Disposition: admitted to medicine.

documents.title: Discharge summary
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
Admitted 03/29/2024, discharged 04/05/2024.

Principal diagnosis: primary CNS lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell type, right parietal lobe.
Secondary: new-onset seizure; SLE; hypertension; asplenia.

Hospital course: presented after a first seizure with a week of confusion, headache and visual disturbance; exam with left-sided weakness and incoordination. MRI showed a single ring-enhancing right parietal lesion with minimal edema. HIV negative. Lumbar puncture 3/30: WBC 2, protein 38, glucose 61, cytology negative. Stereotactic brain biopsy by neurosurgery 4/1 without complication; pathology diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, consistent with primary CNS lymphoma. Staging CT chest/abdomen/pelvis showed no disease outside the CNS. Ophthalmology slit-lamp exam: no vitreous or retinal involvement. No further seizures on levetiracetam. Confusion improved; left-sided weakness improving with PT.

Discharge medications: NEW levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily. Continue hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily, prednisone 10 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg, amlodipine 5 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, potassium chloride 20 mEq, cholecalciferol, calcium carbonate.
Allergies: sulfonamides.

Follow-up: neuro-oncology 4/12 to begin methotrexate-based chemotherapy. PCP within one week. No driving for six months after a seizure (Massachusetts law); patient and husband informed.

Hospital Medicine

documents.title: Call with hospital team
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Husband called the office - she had the brain biopsy yesterday, waiting on pathology. Spoke with the inpatient attending: preliminary read favors lymphoma, final pending; staging CTs tomorrow; oncology already involved. Gave them our direct line. Called husband back, offered support; will see her within a week of discharge.

documents.title: Post-hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Here with husband after admission 3/29-4/5. Seizure, solitary R parietal lesion; biopsy 4/1 = primary CNS lymphoma (DLBCL). Staging negative. Levetiracetam started. Discharge summary and path reviewed.

She is clearer. L hand still weaker, doing home exercises. No further seizures. Mild headache, Tylenol helps. Scared but ready to start treatment Friday. Husband driving her; she understands no driving 6 months.

Exam: alert, oriented x3, speech fluent. L grip 4/5, L finger-nose slightly clumsy. Biopsy site clean. Heart RRR. Lungs clear.

A/P:
1. PCNSL - oncology 4/12 to start high-dose MTX-based chemo. We'll coordinate; she can message any time.
2. Seizure - levetiracetam 500 bid, tolerating. No driving.
3. SLE - HCQ + pred 10 continue; rheum informed.
4. HTN - BP OK today. Watch K and Cr closely with MTX - oncology will draw.
5. Work: off for treatment, will complete leave forms.
Took time to talk through questions. RTC 2-3 months or as needed; telehealth fine during chemo.

Outside oncology center, neuro-oncology. Seen 04/12/2024.

Dear Doctor,

Ms. Diallo is a 47-year-old with SLE on hydroxychloroquine and prednisone 10 mg, asplenia after a 2023 splenic rupture, and newly diagnosed primary CNS lymphoma (diffuse large B-cell) of the right parietal lobe, diagnosed by stereotactic biopsy 4/1/2024 after presenting with a seizure. Staging CT and slit-lamp exam showed no disease outside the brain; CSF cytology was negative.

She is recovering well from the admission and her left-sided weakness is improving.

Plan: induction with high-dose methotrexate and rituximab every two weeks for six cycles, starting today, as an inpatient for each methotrexate infusion with leucovorin rescue and level monitoring. If she responds, consolidation with high-dose cytarabine. We will reimage after induction. Continue levetiracetam. Hydroxychloroquine and prednisone continue; we have spoken with her rheumatologist. No live vaccines.

Allergies: sulfonamides.

Neuro-Oncology

documents.title: Emergency department physician note
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Hospital ED, seen Sunday 04/05/2026 11:50.

CC: weak, dark urine, spots on legs.

HPI: 49F with SLE (hydroxychloroquine, prednisone 10 mg), asplenia since 2023, primary CNS lymphoma in remission. Three days of generalized weakness, urine the color of tea, and a new rash of tiny red-purple dots on both lower legs. Started on hydralazine about three weeks ago for blood pressure.

Meds: hydralazine 25 mg TID (new), lisinopril 20, amlodipine 5, HCTZ 25, KCl 20 mEq, hydroxychloroquine 200 bid, prednisone 10, cholecalciferol, calcium carbonate.
Allergy: sulfonamides.

Vitals: T 37.8 C, BP 150/90, HR 110, RR 20.
Exam: tired, jaundiced, scleral icterus. Petechiae over both lower legs. Abdomen soft, healed LUQ scar. Heart tachycardic, regular. Lungs clear. Neuro nonfocal.

Labs: Hgb 8.0, platelets 40, LDH 700, total bilirubin 3.2 (direct 0.8), haptoglobin <10. Smear: schistocytes present. Creatinine 0.9. DAT negative.

MDM: hemolysis with schistocytes and thrombocytopenia, low-grade temperature, tachycardia. TTP must be excluded; recent hydralazine is a candidate drug cause. Hydralazine held. ADAMTS13 sent. Hematology consulted from the ED. Asplenic with temperature 37.8: cultures drawn, observed closely.

Disposition: admitted to medicine, telemetry.

documents.title: Discharge summary
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
Admitted 04/05/2026. Discharged 04/09/2026.

Diagnoses: drug-induced hemolytic anemia with thrombocytopenia, attributed to hydralazine. SLE, hypertension, asplenia, history of primary CNS lymphoma.

Course: presented with weakness, dark urine and lower-leg petechiae three weeks after starting hydralazine. Hgb 8.0, platelets 40, LDH 700, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, haptoglobin undetectable, schistocytes on smear. DAT negative. Creatinine normal throughout. Hematology saw her on arrival; with a rapid ADAMTS13 activity of 64% resulting on day 2, TTP was excluded and plasma exchange was not started. Hydralazine was stopped on admission and not restarted. Blood cultures no growth. No transfusion required. Hemolysis markers and platelets improved daily: at discharge Hgb 8.7, platelets 96, LDH 430, total bilirubin 1.7. Prednisone continued at her usual 10 mg.

NEW ALLERGY: hydralazine (drug-induced hemolysis). Do not rechallenge.

Discharge medications: STOP hydralazine. Continue lisinopril 20, amlodipine 5, hydrochlorothiazide 25, potassium chloride 20 mEq, hydroxychloroquine 200 mg bid, prednisone 10 mg, cholecalciferol, calcium carbonate.

Follow-up: PCP within one week with CBC, LDH and bilirubin. Hematology as needed. Blood pressure regimen to be adjusted by PCP.

Hospital Medicine
